items.prompt: A platform team writes a deploy script that only works because it hardcodes one team's exact repo layout and Terraform variables. What's missing for this to count as a platform, not a product?
choices: Nothing — it deploys successfully, so it's already a platform
It needs to generalize the pattern so other teams can reuse it without the platform team hand-holding each one
It needs to be rewritten in a different programming language
It needs a prettier README
items.explanation: Working for one team is a product outcome, not a platform outcome. A platform requires the common pattern to be extracted and packaged so any team can self-serve it — the script encoding one team's specific assumptions as if they were universal is exactly what blocks reuse.
items.reference:
🛠️ Product: solves one customer's exact problem
🛣️ Platform: solves the class of problem, self-service for any team

Why: a script that only works for its first user hasn't generalized the pattern yet — it's a product with one customer, not a platform.

items.prompt: Two platform teams both shipped a 'deploy service.' Team A's is used only by the team that requested it and needs a platform engineer present for every new integration. Team B's is used by 20 teams with zero platform-team involvement per onboarding. Which one is actually operating as a platform?
choices: Team A, because they shipped first
Team B, because adoption happens without the platform team in the room
Both equally, since both technically deploy services
Neither, since platforms require a dedicated portal UI
items.explanation: A platform is defined by teams being able to self-serve it, not by whether it technically works. Team A's tool still routes every new adopter through the platform team, which is the ticket-driven, bottlenecked pattern the unit opens with — Team B's is the actual platform behavior.
items.reference:
🛠️ Product: solves one customer's exact problem
🛣️ Platform: solves the class of problem, self-service for any team

Why: a script that only works for its first user hasn't generalized the pattern yet — it's a product with one customer, not a platform.

items.prompt: Why does treating other engineering teams as 'customers' matter for a platform team, rather than just treating them as internal requesters?
choices: It doesn't — internal teams don't need the same rigor external customers get
It means adoption, feedback, and time-to-value get evaluated the same way product work is, instead of just 'did it technically ship'
It's only a branding exercise for the platform team's own morale
It means the platform team should charge other teams money for usage
items.explanation: Framing other teams as customers is what pulls in a real feedback loop and adoption metrics — the same discipline a product team applies to end users — instead of a platform team assuming 'we built it, it must be good' the way the original bespoke script was.
items.reference:
🛠️ Product: solves one customer's exact problem
🛣️ Platform: solves the class of problem, self-service for any team

Why: a script that only works for its first user hasn't generalized the pattern yet — it's a product with one customer, not a platform.

items.prompt: What best describes a 'paved road' or 'golden path' in platform engineering?
choices: The only legally allowed way to build and ship a service
The default, supported, self-service way to do a common task — with an intentional way off it
A one-time onboarding checklist a human walks new teams through
A style guide with no tooling behind it
items.explanation: A paved road is a default a team can walk without asking permission, not a mandate. It stays a road (optional, supported) rather than becoming a prison (forced, no way off) precisely because it ships with a documented escape hatch.
items.reference:
🛣️ Paved road = default + supported + self-service
🚪 + a documented, intentional way off it

Why: remove the way off and a paved road becomes a paved prison — teams with a real reason to deviate fork around it instead.

items.prompt: A platform team publishes a golden-path CI template but blocks any service from shipping unless it uses that exact template, with no documented exception process. What have they actually built?
choices: A paved road, since it's opinionated and consistent
A paved prison, since there's no legitimate way off it
A platform API, since it's automated
A service catalog, since it tracks services
items.explanation: A golden path without any documented way to deviate isn't optional anymore — it's mandatory, and teams with a genuine reason to deviate will do so quietly instead of visibly, which is the exact 'paved prison' failure mode the unit calls out.
items.reference:
🛣️ Paved road = default + supported + self-service
🚪 + a documented, intentional way off it

Why: remove the way off and a paved road becomes a paved prison — teams with a real reason to deviate fork around it instead.

items.prompt: Why should a paved road include a documented escape hatch instead of just being mandatory for everyone?
choices: So the platform team has less work to review
So teams with a genuine reason to deviate do so visibly and supported, instead of forking quietly and invisibly
Escape hatches are only needed for legal compliance reasons
So the golden path can be skipped entirely by any team who prefers to
items.explanation: Without a sanctioned exception path, a team with a real reason to deviate still deviates — they just do it without telling anyone, which the platform team only discovers later when it breaks. A documented escape hatch keeps that deviation visible and supported.
items.reference:
👁️ Documented escape hatch: platform team knows it exists
🕳️ No escape hatch: teams fork silently, invisibly

Why: a visible, sanctioned off-ramp is strictly better than an invisible one — the platform team can't manage what it can't see.

items.prompt: A team has an unusual compliance requirement the golden path CI template doesn't support. With a documented escape hatch process, what's the right next step?
choices: The team is blocked entirely until the platform team rebuilds the template for them
The team silently copies the template and modifies it without telling anyone
The team declares the deviation through the supported exception process, and it becomes visible and trackable
The team abandons the golden path concept for the whole org
items.explanation: A supported escape-hatch process exists so a legitimate deviation gets recorded, not hidden — the team keeps moving, and the platform team retains visibility into who's off the paved road and why, instead of finding out only when something breaks.
items.reference:
👁️ Documented escape hatch: platform team knows it exists
🕳️ No escape hatch: teams fork silently, invisibly

Why: a visible, sanctioned off-ramp is strictly better than an invisible one — the platform team can't manage what it can't see.

items.prompt: What's the actual risk of a golden path having zero documented way to opt out?
choices: Nothing — a strict mandate always produces more consistency
Teams that genuinely need to deviate do it anyway, just without informing the platform team, so the fork is undocumented and unmaintained
It only risks the platform team's morale, not the codebase
It guarantees 100% adoption forever
items.explanation: Removing the legal way off a mandatory path doesn't remove teams' real reasons to deviate — it just removes the platform team's visibility into when that happens, producing worse, unmanaged drift instead of the intended consistency.
items.reference:
👁️ Documented escape hatch: platform team knows it exists
🕳️ No escape hatch: teams fork silently, invisibly

Why: a visible, sanctioned off-ramp is strictly better than an invisible one — the platform team can't manage what it can't see.

items.prompt: Why does a ticket-driven onboarding process put the platform team's headcount on the critical path of every other team's work?
choices: Because tickets are always assigned to the most senior engineer
Because every requesting team has to wait for a platform engineer's availability before they can proceed, no matter how simple the request
Because tickets cost money to file
Because self-service tools are always slower than a human
items.explanation: Any step that requires a human from the platform team to act before a requesting team can move forward makes the platform team's availability a hard dependency for everyone else's progress — self-service removes that dependency for the cases the paved road already covers.
items.reference:
🎫 Ticket-driven: every request waits on a platform engineer
🚶 Self-service: a team walks the road with nobody in the room

Why: self-service removes the platform team from the critical path for the cases the paved road already covers.

items.prompt: A platform team hires two more engineers to answer onboarding tickets faster, without changing how onboarding works. What actually happens to the bottleneck?
choices: It disappears completely — more people means no more waiting
It shrinks proportionally to headcount and stays fixed forever
It just moves — the platform team can now handle more tickets per week, but every new team still waits on a platform engineer's availability
It becomes the requesting teams' problem entirely
items.explanation: Adding headcount to a ticket queue increases throughput but doesn't remove the dependency itself — every team still needs a platform engineer in the loop. Only self-service removes the platform team from the path; more hands just processes the same bottleneck faster.
items.reference:
🎫 Ticket-driven: every request waits on a platform engineer
🚶 Self-service: a team walks the road with nobody in the room

Why: self-service removes the platform team from the critical path for the cases the paved road already covers.

items.prompt: A platform team wants to decide what infrastructure to build next. Which signal should drive that decision under a 'thinnest viable platform' approach?
choices: Whichever infrastructure looks most impressive on a roadmap slide
Friction that's already been observed — e.g. three teams independently writing near-identical setup code
Whatever the platform team personally finds most interesting to build
The newest tooling trend in the industry
items.explanation: Thinnest viable platform means building only what's proven needed by real, observed friction — not speculative infrastructure built ahead of any team asking for it. Three teams independently reinventing the same thing is exactly that signal.
items.reference:
✅ Built from observed friction (3 teams hit the same wall)
❌ Built from a hunch about future needs

Why: a platform roadmap driven by where tickets and workarounds already are stays grounded in real demand, not speculation.

items.prompt: A platform engineer proposes building a general-purpose multi-cloud abstraction layer because 'we might need it someday,' even though every team today only uses one cloud provider. Does this fit the thinnest-viable-platform approach?
choices: Yes — building ahead of need is always the safer choice
No — it's speculative infrastructure built ahead of any observed friction, which is the pattern this approach specifically avoids
Yes, as long as it's well-documented
It's neutral — thinnest viable platform doesn't apply to infrastructure choices
items.explanation: Thinnest viable platform means building the minimum that removes friction actually observed today, not infrastructure justified only by a hypothetical future need nobody has hit yet — that's precisely the speculative-build pattern it warns against.
items.reference:
✅ Built from observed friction (3 teams hit the same wall)
❌ Built from a hunch about future needs

Why: a platform roadmap driven by where tickets and workarounds already are stays grounded in real demand, not speculation.

items.prompt: Why does 'thinnest viable platform' specifically say 'thinnest,' rather than just 'build a good platform'?
choices: It's a marketing term with no practical meaning
It means the platform team should minimize scope to what's proven necessary, since every extra piece built is also a piece the platform team must maintain forever
It means the platform should use the fewest possible programming languages
It refers only to the thickness of documentation, not scope
items.explanation: 'Thinnest' is a deliberate constraint: every capability the platform team builds becomes something they own and maintain indefinitely, so scope should track proven need, not aspiration — building more than what's needed adds maintenance burden without proportional benefit.
items.reference:
✅ Built from observed friction (3 teams hit the same wall)
❌ Built from a hunch about future needs

Why: a platform roadmap driven by where tickets and workarounds already are stays grounded in real demand, not speculation.

items.prompt: In the layered internal developer platform (infra → platform APIs → golden-path templates → developer portal), what breaks if the platform APIs layer still requires a human to manually approve every call?
choices: Nothing breaks — only the top-most portal layer needs to be self-service
The golden-path templates above it stop being truly self-service, since they now silently depend on that human's availability
It only affects the infra layer below it
It makes the golden-path templates faster, since a human double-checks correctness
items.explanation: Self-service has to hold all the way down the stack. If the layer beneath the one a developer directly touches secretly requires a human, the layer above only looks self-service — the bottleneck has just relocated one layer down, not disappeared.
items.reference:
📱 Portal → 🛣️ Golden paths → 🔌 Platform APIs → ☁️ Infra

Why: every layer above only stays self-service if every layer below it actually is too — one hidden manual step anywhere in the stack relocates the bottleneck, it doesn't remove it.

items.prompt: What's the role of the 'platform APIs' layer specifically, distinct from raw infrastructure below it and golden-path templates above it?
choices: It's purely a documentation layer with no code
It wraps raw infrastructure behind callable, automated operations (like 'provision a database') that a script can call without a human
It's identical to the developer portal, just under a different name
It replaces the need for infrastructure entirely
items.explanation: Platform APIs are what turn raw infrastructure into something a golden-path template can call programmatically — 'provision a Postgres instance' as a callable operation, not a ticket. Without this layer, golden-path templates would have nothing self-service to call.
items.reference:
📱 Portal → 🛣️ Golden paths → 🔌 Platform APIs → ☁️ Infra

Why: every layer above only stays self-service if every layer below it actually is too — one hidden manual step anywhere in the stack relocates the bottleneck, it doesn't remove it.

items.prompt: Why does the developer portal / service catalog layer matter, given that the golden-path templates below it already do the actual provisioning work?
choices: It doesn't matter — templates alone are sufficient
It makes the golden path discoverable and records ownership/status, without which teams don't know it exists and nobody can answer 'who owns this' later
It's only a cosmetic dashboard with no functional role
It replaces the need for golden-path templates
items.explanation: A golden path that works but isn't discoverable might as well not exist for teams who don't know about it, and without a catalog recording ownership, that data rots the moment a team reorganizes — the portal layer is what keeps the platform usable and its metadata trustworthy over time.
items.reference:
📱 Portal → 🛣️ Golden paths → 🔌 Platform APIs → ☁️ Infra

Why: every layer above only stays self-service if every layer below it actually is too — one hidden manual step anywhere in the stack relocates the bottleneck, it doesn't remove it.

items.prompt: In the golden-path build loop (observe friction → extract pattern → add guardrails → publish and measure → iterate), what comes right after extracting the common pattern from multiple teams' setups?
choices: Immediately publishing it with no further changes
Adding guardrails — baking in the defaults a security review would otherwise catch late, like least-privilege IAM and required tags
Deleting the original bespoke scripts with no replacement
Skipping straight to measuring adoption before anything is published
items.explanation: After the shared pattern is extracted, the loop adds guardrails so following the paved road is also the compliant path — security defaults and required metadata get baked into the template rather than left as a separate checklist teams might skip.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Observe → 2️⃣ Extract → 3️⃣ Guard → 4️⃣ Publish & measure → 5️⃣ Iterate

Why: the loop doesn't end at publish — the next friction it surfaces feeds back into step 1, which is what keeps the platform demand-driven instead of one-and-done.

items.prompt: After a golden-path template is published, what determines whether the loop is actually done, according to the build loop?
choices: Publishing itself is the final step — nothing happens after
Measured adoption and tickets deflected, which then feed new friction back into observing the next thing to build
Whether the platform team feels proud of the work
Whether it was announced in an all-hands meeting
items.explanation: A golden path nobody uses hasn't solved anything — the loop only closes once adoption is measured, and whatever friction that measurement or usage surfaces becomes the input to the next iteration, rather than treating publish as the finish line.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Observe → 2️⃣ Extract → 3️⃣ Guard → 4️⃣ Publish & measure → 5️⃣ Iterate

Why: the loop doesn't end at publish — the next friction it surfaces feeds back into step 1, which is what keeps the platform demand-driven instead of one-and-done.

items.prompt: What does 'platform as a product' concretely require a platform team to do that a purely infrastructure-focused team might skip?
choices: Add a paid pricing tier for internal teams
Track adoption, gather feedback from the teams using it, and evaluate 'done' by outcomes like time-to-first-deploy, not just technical function
Only ship features that are technically impressive
Avoid ever changing the platform once it ships
items.explanation: Treating other teams as customers pulls in product discipline — adoption tracking, a feedback loop, and outcome metrics — instead of stopping at 'does it technically work,' which is the same gap that let the original bespoke script go unnoticed as a bottleneck.
items.reference:
📊 Coverage % · ⏱️ Time-to-first-deploy · 🎫 Tickets deflected · 🙋 Voluntary adoption

Why: these four numbers are what tell a platform team whether the fix actually worked, instead of assuming it did because it shipped.

items.prompt: A platform team ships a new self-service tool and moves on to the next project without checking whether any team actually uses it. What's missing from their process?
choices: Nothing — shipping is the only thing that matters
The feedback loop and adoption measurement that platform-as-product thinking requires — without it, they can't tell if it actually solved anything
A bigger marketing budget
A rename of the tool to something catchier
items.explanation: Without measuring adoption, the platform team has no way to know whether the tool reduced friction or just added another option nobody uses — the same blind spot that let the original one-off Payments script go six months without anyone noticing it didn't generalize.
items.reference:
📊 Coverage % · ⏱️ Time-to-first-deploy · 🎫 Tickets deflected · 🙋 Voluntary adoption

Why: these four numbers are what tell a platform team whether the fix actually worked, instead of assuming it did because it shipped.

items.prompt: Which pair of metrics together best tells a platform team whether a golden path is genuinely working, not just technically deployed?
choices: Lines of code in the template, and number of platform-team commits
Voluntary adoption rate, and time-to-first-deploy for a new service
How many meetings were held to design it
The number of cloud regions it supports
items.explanation: Voluntary adoption shows teams are choosing the road rather than being forced onto it, and time-to-first-deploy shows it's actually faster than the old way — together they measure real outcomes, unlike proxies like code volume or meeting count.
items.reference:
📊 Coverage % · ⏱️ Time-to-first-deploy · 🎫 Tickets deflected · 🙋 Voluntary adoption

Why: these four numbers are what tell a platform team whether the fix actually worked, instead of assuming it did because it shipped.

items.prompt: A platform team makes their CI template mandatory with no opt-out and later discovers two teams silently forked it and stopped updating. What does this reveal about mandates vs. guardrails?
choices: The mandate worked exactly as intended
Removing the legitimate escape hatch didn't remove teams' real reasons to deviate — it only removed the platform team's visibility into it
The two teams should be immediately shut down
Mandatory templates always increase consistency with no downside
items.explanation: A mandate with no legal way off pushes real deviations underground where they drift unnoticed — a documented, supported escape hatch would have kept the same deviation visible and trackable instead, which is a better consistency outcome than an invisible fork.
items.reference:
🚦 Guardrail: opinionated default + supported opt-out
🚫 Mandate: forced, no legal way off

Why: a road earns adoption by being easier than the alternative — being the only legal option just pushes real deviations underground.

items.prompt: What's the difference between a 'guardrail' and a 'mandate' in the context of a golden path?
choices: They're the same thing, just different words for the same policy
A guardrail is an opinionated default a team can still opt out of with support; a mandate forces adoption with no legitimate way off
A guardrail only applies to security, a mandate only applies to CI
A mandate is always technical, a guardrail is always organizational
items.explanation: A guardrail keeps the road paved but optional — it earns adoption by being the easier path, with a supported way off for teams that genuinely need one. A mandate removes that option entirely, which is what pushes real deviations into invisible forks.
items.reference:
🚦 Guardrail: opinionated default + supported opt-out
🚫 Mandate: forced, no legal way off

Why: a road earns adoption by being easier than the alternative — being the only legal option just pushes real deviations underground.

items.prompt: What core problem does a service catalog solve that golden-path templates alone don't?
choices: It makes the CI pipeline run faster
It makes the golden path discoverable and records ownership/tier metadata, which templates alone don't track over time
It replaces the need for platform APIs
It automatically writes new golden-path templates
items.explanation: A template can provision a service correctly and still leave no durable record of who owns it, what tier it is, or that it exists at all — the catalog is what makes that metadata queryable and keeps 'who owns this' answerable months later.
items.reference:
🔍 Discoverable: teams can find the paved road
🏷️ Ownership: ownership/tier metadata stays queryable

Why: a paved road nobody can find, or whose ownership data has rotted, is functionally invisible even if the underlying template still works.

items.prompt: A team disbands four months after their service was scaffolded via the golden path. What keeps the catalog's 'owner' field from silently going stale in a case like this?
choices: Nothing — catalog data never needs to be checked once written
A periodic reconciliation process that cross-checks recorded owners against a live team registry and flags mismatches
The golden-path template itself automatically detects team disbandment
Catalog entries expire and delete themselves after 90 days
items.explanation: Catalog metadata is only as accurate as the last update — without a periodic check against a source of truth for team existence, ownership silently becomes aspirational rather than accurate, exactly the failure mode L3 calls out.
items.reference:
🔍 Discoverable: teams can find the paved road
🏷️ Ownership: ownership/tier metadata stays queryable

Why: a paved road nobody can find, or whose ownership data has rotted, is functionally invisible even if the underlying template still works.

items.prompt: Why does the developer portal / service catalog sit at the top of the layered IDP diagram, above golden-path templates?
choices: Because it's the least important layer
Because it's the layer teams actually interact with to discover and understand what's available, built on top of everything underneath actually working
Because it runs before the infrastructure layer provisions anything
Layer order in the diagram has no meaning
items.explanation: The portal is the visible, discoverable surface of the whole stack — it only works if every layer beneath it (golden paths, platform APIs, infrastructure) is functioning and self-service, which is why it sits on top rather than being a standalone piece.
items.reference:
🔍 Discoverable: teams can find the paved road
🏷️ Ownership: ownership/tier metadata stays queryable

Why: a paved road nobody can find, or whose ownership data has rotted, is functionally invisible even if the underlying template still works.

items.prompt: Implement `renderTemplate(template, vars)` which replaces every `{{key}}` placeholder in `template` with `vars[key]`, leaving unrecognized placeholders untouched (matching L3's `renderTemplate`).
items.explanation: A regex finds every {{key}} placeholder; the replacer function looks key up in vars and substitutes it when present, or returns the original match unchanged when it's missing. This is the mechanism behind every scaffolding tool: fill placeholders from one source of truth (the manifest) rather than hand-typing per-team values into a copy.
items.reference:
📝 template: 'Hi {{name}}'
🔤 vars: { name: 'Ada' }
➡️ output: 'Hi Ada'

Why: a scaffolder generates files by filling placeholders from one manifest, so every generated file stays consistent instead of hand-copied and drifting.

items.prompt: Implement `isSupportedVersion(version, minMajor)` which returns `true` if `version` (a 'X.Y.Z' string) has a major number `>= minMajor`, and `false` otherwise (including for malformed strings).
items.explanation: A regex first confirms the string is valid semver shape and captures the major number; if it doesn't match, the version is treated as unsupported rather than crashing. This mirrors L3's validateManifest check that flags services still on a deprecated golden-path major version instead of silently letting them drift.
items.reference:
✅ 'is this manifest compliant' becomes a function call
🚫 not 'ask a human to read the code'

Why: a machine-checkable validator is what lets a CI gate or nightly audit catch drift automatically, instead of relying on a person noticing.

items.explanation: Checking both falsy values and a trimmed-empty string catches missing owners and 'owner: "   "' alike, returning a list of errors rather than a single boolean — the same shape as L3's validateManifest, which accumulates every problem found instead of stopping at the first one.
